implementation_notes: jest.spyOn replaces one method on an object with a mock function that still calls the original implementation by default - the runner's built-in spy - so the test runs the real code path and then asserts with toHaveBeenCalled/toHaveBeenCalledWith/toHaveBeenCalledTimes, restoring via jest.restoreAllMocks() in afterEach. What replaces the classic spy object is the runner's mock-function machinery attached to the real method; mockImplementation()/mockReturnValue() turn it into a stub only where the test needs that.
pitfalls: Unlike sinon, jest.spyOn calls the spied method by default, so real side effects run; chain .mockImplementation(() => {}) to neutralise.
Spies patched onto shared objects or module namespaces leak into later tests unless restored; jest.restoreAllMocks only restores spyOn/replaced properties, not jest.mock automocks.
Spying on a value destructured at import time records nothing: the SUT must reach the method through the spied object at call time.

variants.name: Sinon.JS spy (records arguments, return value, this, exception)
variants.implementation_notes: A sinon spy is a function that records arguments, return value, this and thrown exception for every call; sinon.spy(obj, 'method') wraps an existing method and delegates by default, sandbox.restore() puts the original back, and assertions use sinon.assert.calledOnceWithExactly or matchers over spy.getCalls(). What replaces the classic spy object is the instrumented function; sinon's own docs now recommend sinon.fake() for new code, which records in the same way.
pitfalls: Without a sandbox each spy must be restored individually, or the original method stays wrapped for later tests.
An anonymous sinon.spy() records but does nothing; use sinon.spy(realFn) or sinon.fake(realFn) when the behaviour must actually run.
In async code, assert after awaiting the operation - sinon assertion failures and the spied function's own errors are otherwise easy to conflate.
